draft.title: Approximate confidence intervals
card: A confidence interval gives a range of likely values for the population proportion p. First find p-hat = x ÷ n, where x is the number with the feature and n is the sample size.
An approximate 95% confidence interval for p is p-hat ± 1.96 × √(p-hat(1 − p-hat)/n). Work out the part after ± first. It is the margin of error.
Worked example: 20 of 100 people are left-handed. p-hat = 0.2, so √(0.2 × 0.8 ÷ 100) = √0.0016 = 0.04.
The margin of error is 1.96 × 0.04 = 0.0784. The interval is 0.2 ± 0.0784, which is about 0.122 to 0.278.
draft.remember: Find p-hat, then p-hat ± 1.96 × √(p-hat(1 − p-hat)/n), with n the sample size.

a.q: In a survey of 400 Victorian students, 100 walk to school. What is the approximate 95% confidence interval for p?
a.why: p-hat = 100 ÷ 400 = 0.25. The margin is 1.96 × √(0.25 × 0.75 ÷ 400) ≈ 0.042, giving 0.208 to 0.292. Leaving out 1.96 gives a narrower interval, 0.228 to 0.272, which is not the 95% interval.
a.clue: Find p-hat first, then divide by the sample size inside the root.

b.q: A council surveys 900 residents of Ballarat, and 540 say they use the library. What is the margin of error for a 95% interval for p, to 3 decimal places?
b.why: p-hat = 540 ÷ 900 = 0.6, and n = 900. The margin is 1.96 × √(0.6 × 0.4 ÷ 900) ≈ 0.032. Using 540 as n gives 0.041, which mixes up the count with the sample size.
b.clue: n is the number surveyed, not the number who said yes.

check.summary: No problems found. The card's worked example and both questions' arithmetic check out, and the distractors match common errors (wrong n, or leaving out 1.96).

final.title: Approximate confidence intervals
card: A confidence interval gives a range of likely values for the population proportion \(p\). First find \(\hat{p} = \frac{x}{n}\), where \(x\) is the number with the feature and \(n\) is the sample size.
An approximate 95% confidence interval for \(p\) is \(\hat{p} \pm 1.96 \times \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1 - \hat{p})}{n}}\). Work out the part after \(\pm\) first. It is the margin of error.
Worked example: 20 of 100 people are left-handed. \(\hat{p} = 0.2\), so \(\sqrt{\frac{0.2 \times 0.8}{100}} = \sqrt{0.0016} = 0.04\).
The margin of error is \(1.96 \times 0.04 = 0.0784\). The interval is \(0.2 \pm 0.0784\), which is about 0.122 to 0.278.
final.remember: Find \(\hat{p}\), then \(\hat{p} \pm 1.96 \times \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1 - \hat{p})}{n}}\), with \(n\) the sample size.

a.q: In a survey of 400 Victorian students, 100 walk to school. What is the approximate 95% confidence interval for \(p\)?
a.why: \(\hat{p} = \frac{100}{400} = 0.25\). The margin is \(1.96 \times \sqrt{\frac{0.25 \times 0.75}{400}} \approx 0.042\), giving 0.208 to 0.292. Leaving out 1.96 gives a narrower interval, 0.228 to 0.272, which is not the 95% interval.
a.clue: Find \(\hat{p}\) first, then divide by the sample size inside the root.

b.q: A council surveys 900 residents of Ballarat, and 540 say they use the library. What is the margin of error for a 95% interval for \(p\), to 3 decimal places?
b.why: \(\hat{p} = \frac{540}{900} = 0.6\), and \(n = 900\). The margin is \(1.96 \times \sqrt{\frac{0.6 \times 0.4}{900}} \approx 0.032\). Using 540 as \(n\) gives 0.041, which mixes up the count with the sample size.
b.clue: \(n\) is the number surveyed, not the number who said yes.
